name: Sun and planet gear
summary: A planet gear fixed to a beam engine's connecting rod orbits a sun gear on the flywheel shaft, turning the shaft twice per orbit.

ratio.typical: shaft turns = 1 + zp/zs per planet orbit; 2 turns per beam double stroke with equal gears

topology.notes: ground, beam, connecting rod with planet rigidly fixed, sun with flywheel, retaining link from sun shaft to planet centre; one gear mesh

explain.motion: The beam rocks and drives the connecting rod, whose lower end carries a planet gear that cannot turn relative to the rod. A retaining link keeps the planet in mesh as its centre orbits the sun gear on the flywheel shaft. Because the planet does not spin on its own axis, the sun is driven round by both the orbit and the rolling mesh, so with equal gears the shaft makes two turns per orbit.
explain.forces: The rod thrust acts at the mesh, tangential to the sun, so torque is the rod force times the pitch radius of the sun, varying with rod angle like a crank. The retaining link carries the radial separating force; the gear teeth and the link pivot are the weak points under shock.
explain.benefits: Gets rotary output from a reciprocating beam without a crank and doubles shaft speed compared with a crank. It has no dead centre in the way a single crank does at top and bottom.
explain.limits: More parts, gear wear and backlash than a simple crank, and the flywheel is still needed to smooth the torque. It fell out of use once the crank patent expired around 1794.

build.ground: engine frame with beam pivot O_b and flywheel shaft O_s
build.input: beam, oscillating about O_b by about ±24° (or drive the planet orbit angle directly for animation)
build.output: sun gear and flywheel, rotation about O_s

members.def: beam pivot O_b at (0, 520), sun shaft O_s at (300, 0)
O_b to beam end B, length 300 mm, oscillating
B to planet centre P, length 400 mm; planet gear rigidly fixed at P (no rotation relative to rod)
z = 24, module 5, pitch radius 60 mm, part of rod
z = 24, module 5, pitch radius 60 mm, on flywheel shaft O_s
O_s to P, length 120 mm = sun + planet pitch radii, keeps gears in mesh

params.name: L
params.note: connecting rod length B to P

build.defining_relations: Planet does not rotate in the frame of the rod. Willis: (w_s - w_r)/(w_p - w_r) = -zp/zs with w_r the retainer (orbit) speed. If the rod barely rotates (w_p about 0), w_s = w_r (1 + zp/zs). Equal gears give 2:1. Orbit radius c = m(zs+zp)/2; beam end vertical travel = 2c.
build.range: planet orbits 360° continuously; beam swings about ±24°; sun turns 720° per orbit
build.plot: sun angle vs orbit angle (nearly straight line of slope 2, with small ripple from rod tilt)
build.notes: Planet angle equals rod angle, not orbit angle. Keep tooth phase consistent: sun angle = orbit angle + (zp/zs)(orbit angle - rod angle). The direction of rotation depends on which side of the sun the planet starts on during the down stroke; a flywheel carries it through.

name: Wankel rotary engine
summary: A triangular rotor orbits inside an epitrochoid housing, phased by a 3:2 internal gear, turning the eccentric shaft three times per rotor turn.

ratio.typical: eccentric shaft 3 turns per rotor turn (rotor gear : fixed gear = 3:2)

topology.notes: ground (housing with fixed external gear), eccentric shaft, rotor with internal gear; one gear mesh; apex seals sliding on the housing are redundant contacts

explain.motion: The rotor's internal gear rolls on a fixed gear on the housing, so the rotor centre orbits the shaft axis on the eccentric while the rotor turns slowly the same way. Its three apexes stay on the epitrochoid wall, forming three chambers that grow and shrink twice per rotor turn. The eccentric shaft turns three times for each rotor revolution, giving one power stroke per shaft turn per rotor.
explain.forces: Gas pressure on each rotor flank pushes through the rotor bearing onto the eccentric, producing torque equal to force times eccentricity. The phasing gears carry only the reaction that keeps the rotor in step, while apex seals take sliding contact loads and wear.
explain.benefits: Very compact and smooth for its power, with no reciprocating parts and few moving pieces.
explain.limits: Long thin combustion chambers burn poorly, giving higher fuel use and emissions. Apex seal wear and oil consumption limit life.

build.ground: housing with epitrochoid bore and fixed external phasing gear coaxial with the shaft
build.input: eccentric shaft, continuous rotation (in the engine the rotor gas forces drive it; for animation drive the shaft)
build.output: rotor position and chamber volumes; shaft torque

members.def: epitrochoid x = e cos3a + R cos a, y = e sin3a + R sin a, with R = 103, e = 15
external gear z = 30, module 2, pitch radius 30, fixed to housing at origin
eccentric shaft, journal offset e = 15 mm from origin
curved triangle, apex radius R = 103 mm from rotor centre; internal gear z = 45, pitch radius 45

params.name: R
params.note: generating radius (rotor centre to apex), Mazda 13B-REW

build.defining_relations: Rotor angle = shaft angle / 3. Rotor centre = e(cos t, sin t). Apex k at angle t/3 + k*120° at distance R from rotor centre traces the epitrochoid. Gear centre distance e = m(z_rotor - z_fixed)/2 and z_rotor/z_fixed = 3/2. K = R/e about 6.9 (must exceed about 6 for a usable chamber).
build.range: shaft 360° continuous; rotor turns 120° per shaft turn; each chamber goes through intake, compression, power, exhaust over 1080° of shaft
build.plot: chamber volume vs shaft angle for one chamber
build.notes: Draw rotor flanks as arcs slightly inside the inner envelope so they clear the housing waist. Rotor and shaft turn the same direction. Ports and spark plugs are static decoration.

name: Ravigneaux planetary gearset
summary: Two suns, short and long pinions on one carrier and a single ring give several forward ratios and reverse in a compact automatic gearbox.

topology.notes: ground, small sun, large sun, carrier, short pinion, long pinion, ring (one pinion of each set shown, usually 3 of each); meshes: small sun-short, short-long, long-large sun, long-ring

explain.motion: Short pinions mesh with the small sun and with the long pinions; long pinions mesh with the large sun and the ring. All pinions ride on one carrier. Holding one member with a brake and driving another fixes the ratio between input and output, so clutches and bands select the gear.
explain.forces: Torque splits between three pinion pairs, so tooth loads are shared and the unit carries high torque for its size. The held member's brake takes the reaction torque; the short-to-long pinion meshes see the highest tooth loads in low gear.
explain.benefits: Gives three or four forward speeds and reverse from one compact coaxial gearset with fewer parts than two simple planetaries.
explain.limits: Ratio spacing is constrained by shared tooth counts, and the long pinions and their bearings are a weak point. Shifts need coordinated clutch and brake timing.

build.ground: transmission case with brakes able to hold the large sun, the carrier or the ring
build.input: small sun (forward) or large sun (reverse), continuous rotation

members.def: z = 30, module 2, pitch radius 30 mm at origin
z = 36, pitch radius 36 mm at origin (axially offset)
holds short pinions at radius 48 and long pinions at radius 60, 44.05° apart
z = 18, pitch radius 18, orbit radius 48
z = 24, pitch radius 24, orbit radius 60
internal z = 84, pitch radius 84 at origin

params.name: n_sets
params.note: pinion pairs around carrier, needs (Ss+R)/3 integer: 38

build.defining_relations: Large sun to ring via one pinion: (wR - wc)/(wSl - wc) = -Sl/R. Small sun to ring via two pinions: (wR - wc)/(wSs - wc) = +Ss/R. Gears: carrier held, input small sun: wR/wSs = Ss/R (1st). Large sun held: wR/wSs = Ss(R+Sl)/(R(Ss+Sl)) (2nd). Any two locked: 1:1 (3rd). Carrier held, input large sun: wR/wSl = -Sl/R (reverse). Geometry: R = Sl + 2Pl; short-long centre spacing (Ps+Pl)m/2 = 42 with orbit radii 48 and 60 gives 44.05° between them.
build.range: all members rotate continuously; ratio depends on which member is held
build.plot: ring speed vs small sun speed for each selected gear (lever diagram)
build.notes: Two DOF until a brake is applied; provide a gear selector that holds one member. Short and long pinions turn opposite ways. Check tooth phasing of 3 pinion pairs; the long pinion is twice the face width so it reaches both the large sun and the short pinion plane.

name: Cam and roller follower
summary: A shaped disc lifts a roller follower along its guide, so the output motion is whatever profile you cut into the cam.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (22 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, cam, follower stem, roller; roller spin is a passive extra freedom; cam contact is the higher pair

explain.motion: As the cam turns, the roller rides its edge and the follower rises and falls along its guide. In this default the profile rises cycloidally over 180° and returns cycloidally over 180°; any timing, including long dwells, can be drawn into the outline.
explain.forces: The cam can only push along the contact normal through the roller centre. The pressure angle between that normal and the follower path decides how much of the push goes sideways into the guide; keep it under about 30°. A spring or gravity must hold the follower on the cam.
explain.benefits: Almost any motion law with two moving parts and exact timing. A roller turns sliding into rolling contact, cutting wear.
explain.limits: Needs a return spring, which can float at high speed. Large lift in a short angle forces a big cam or high pressure angles.

build.ground: frame carrying cam shaft O and two guide blocks for the follower stem (guide from y = 70 to 100 mm)
build.output: follower lift y (roller centre position along the vertical guide)

members.def: profile r(th) = 30 + 22 * s(f), f = th/180° on rise and (360°-th)/180° on return, s cycloidal
vertical stem 70 mm long on the line through O (in-line, zero offset)
roller radius 8 mm pinned at the stem foot

params.name: rb
params.note: base circle radius of cam profile surface

params.name: law
params.note: s(f) = f - sin(2 pi f)/(2 pi)

build.defining_relations: Cycloidal law s = h(f - sin(2 pi f)/(2 pi)), f = theta/beta. The site cuts this law into the cam surface radius and finds lift as the highest roller position touching the profile, so actual lift is close to but not exactly cycloidal. Pressure angle phi = atan(s'/(rb + rr + s)) for an in-line follower; keep phi < 30°.
build.range: cam 360° continuous; follower lift 0 to about 22 mm and back each turn
build.notes: Compute roller contact numerically (envelope); the label turns red past 30° pressure angle. Roller spin is cosmetic. Site rotates cam with th = -u.

examples.detail: Roller lifters follow camshaft lobes to open intake and exhaust valves.

name: Cam with flat-faced follower
summary: A disc cam pushes a follower with a flat face, so contact slides across the face and the push always stays square to the stroke.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (15 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, cam, flat-faced follower; cam contact slides along the face

explain.motion: The cam turns and its lobe pushes the flat face of the follower up its guide. The contact point slides sideways across the face by a distance equal to ds/dtheta. The default profile rises cycloidally over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60°.
explain.forces: The contact normal is always perpendicular to the face, so the pressure angle is zero for an in-line follower and guide side load comes only from friction and contact offset. The sliding contact carries high Hertz stress and needs good lubrication.
explain.benefits: Very compact and stiff with no side thrust from pressure angle, which suits direct-acting engine valves.
explain.limits: The cam must be convex everywhere (no concave flanks), and the face must be wide enough for the contact excursion. Sliding friction causes wear, so flat tappets need careful break-in.

build.ground: frame with cam shaft O and a vertical guide on the line through O

members.def: profile from envelope of follower face lines at distance rb + s(theta) from O
stem with flat face 40 mm wide, face perpendicular to stroke

params.name: face_w
params.note: face width, must exceed 2 x max |ds/dtheta| = 28.6 mm

build.defining_relations: Cam profile point in cam frame: x = (rb + s) sin(theta) + s' cos(theta), y = (rb + s) cos(theta) - s' sin(theta). Contact offset on face = s' = ds/dtheta (max 2h/beta = 14.3 mm). Convexity: radius of curvature rho = rb + s + s'' > 0 everywhere (minimum about 9.9 mm with defaults).
build.range: cam 360° continuous; follower 0 to 15 mm lift, dwells 60° at top and bottom
build.plot: follower lift vs cam angle, with contact offset on the face as a second trace
build.notes: Show the contact point sliding across the face. If params make rho negative the cam would cusp; warn and clamp. In engines the follower is often offset slightly so the tappet spins.

name: Barrel cam
summary: A helical groove around a rotating drum pushes a roller follower back and forth parallel to the drum axis.

ratio.typical: stroke = groove axial travel (40 mm by default) per drum turn

topology.notes: ground, drum, follower slide, roller; roller in groove is a form-closed cam contact

explain.motion: A groove cut around the drum surface wanders along the axis. A roller sitting in the groove is carried with it, so the follower slide moves parallel to the drum axis as the drum turns. The default groove rises over 160°, dwells 20°, returns over 160° and dwells 20°.
explain.forces: Groove walls push both ways, so no return spring is needed. The pressure angle is set by groove slope: tan(phi) = s'/Rp, where Rp is the pitch radius; a larger drum gives a gentler slope and lower side load.
explain.benefits: Positive (form-closed) motion along the shaft axis, compact for long strokes, and can hold several followers on one drum.
explain.limits: Groove backlash means the roller flips walls at reversals, causing wear and noise. Machining a 3D groove is costlier than a plate cam.

build.ground: frame with drum bearings and a slide guide parallel to the drum axis
build.input: drum, continuous rotation about its axis
build.output: follower slide position z along the drum axis

members.def: cylinder radius 50 mm, length 140 mm, groove centreline z(theta) = z0 + s(theta)
carriage on guide parallel to drum axis, carrying radial roller pin
roller dia 12 mm, groove width 12.1 mm, depth 8 mm

build.defining_relations: z = s(theta), cycloidal s = h(f - sin(2 pi f)/(2 pi)). Groove slope ds/dx with x = Rp theta; pressure angle phi = atan(s'/Rp), max s' = 2h/beta = 28.6 mm/rad gives phi max about 30°.
build.range: drum 360° continuous; slide 0 to 40 mm and back per turn
build.plot: slide position vs drum angle (also the unrolled groove)
build.notes: Pseudo-3D: show drum side view with the groove as a sinusoid-like band, or unrolled. The groove must be wider than the roller by a small clearance. Shift drums use stepped dwell grooves instead.

name: Face groove cam
summary: A roller runs in a closed groove cut into the face of a disc, so the cam drives the follower both out and back without a spring.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (20 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, grooved disc, radial follower slide, roller; groove gives form-closed cam contact

explain.motion: The groove is a closed loop machined into the face of the disc; its distance from the centre varies with angle. The roller sits in the groove, so as the disc turns the follower is pulled in and pushed out along its radial guide. The default track rises over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60° with a 3-4-5 polynomial law.
explain.forces: Either groove wall can push, so the follower is driven in both directions and cannot float. Pressure angle limits are the same as a plate cam; the roller reverses which wall it touches when acceleration changes sign.
explain.benefits: Positive motion with no return spring, so it works at high speed and in any orientation.
explain.limits: Roller wall-switching causes backlash, noise and wear, and the roller spins the wrong way when it touches the outer wall. A wider, heavier disc than a plate cam.

build.ground: frame with disc shaft O and a radial guide for the follower

members.def: disc radius 75 mm; groove centreline r(theta) = 35 + s(theta), groove width 10.2 mm
radial slide on a guide through O
roller dia 10 mm in groove

params.name: rb
params.note: base (pitch) circle radius of groove centreline

build.defining_relations: Groove centreline (pitch curve) r = rb + s(theta). Groove walls are offset curves of the pitch curve by ±(groove_w/2). 3-4-5 law max velocity 1.875h/beta. Pressure angle phi = atan(s'/(rb + s)), max about 24° with defaults.
build.range: disc 360° continuous; follower 0 to 20 mm radial travel, dwells 60° at each end
build.notes: Draw both groove walls as offsets of the pitch curve; highlight which wall is in contact (sign of acceleration times load). Minimum radius of curvature of the inner wall must exceed the roller radius.

name: Desmodromic valve cam
summary: Two matched cams and rockers open and close a valve mechanically, so the valve follows the cam with no return spring.

ratio.typical: valve lift 10 mm per cam turn (camshaft at half crank speed)

topology.notes: ground, camshaft (opening and closing lobes), opening rocker, closing rocker, valve; cam-rocker and rocker-valve contacts; deliberately redundant (conjugate) constraint

explain.motion: An opening lobe pushes the opening rocker down onto the valve stem, opening the valve. A second, conjugate closing lobe drives a forked closing rocker that pulls up on a collar on the valve stem, closing it. The two profiles are cut so that at every angle one rocker or the other holds the valve, so lift follows the law exactly.
explain.forces: The opening cam carries gas and inertia loads on opening; the closing cam carries the inertia of deceleration and the closing pull that a spring would normally supply. Rocker sliding contacts carry high loads and need tight clearance control.
explain.benefits: No valve float at high revs and no spring force to overcome, so aggressive lift laws are possible.
explain.limits: Two clearances per valve to set, more parts and sliding friction, and conjugate profiles must be ground very accurately. Modern valve springs and pneumatic returns reduce its advantage.

build.ground: cylinder head with camshaft O, rocker pivots Q1 and Q2 and valve guide
build.output: valve lift y along the guide

members.def: opening lobe (base circle 18 mm, lift 10 mm) and closing lobe (conjugate, base 28 mm) on one shaft
pivot Q1, arm 30 mm to cam pad, arm 30 mm to valve tip (1:1)
pivot Q2, forked arm 30 mm to closing lobe, 30 mm to valve collar (1:1)
stem in guide with split collar, head dia 34 mm

params.name: lash
params.note: closing clearance, valve seated by gas pressure and a light helper spring

build.defining_relations: Valve lift y = s(theta). Opening rocker angle psi1 = asin(y/30) (1:1 rocker) and opening lobe profile is the envelope of the rocker pad at psi1. Closing rocker angle psi2 = -psi1 (forked rocker on opposite side); closing lobe is the envelope of its pad at psi2, so both lobes are conjugate: at every theta both rockers touch their lobes with only lash between.
build.range: camshaft 360° continuous; valve 0 to 10 mm lift in 120° of cam, closed for 240°
build.plot: valve lift vs cam angle, with acceleration showing which rocker carries load
build.notes: Colour the rocker currently carrying load (opening cam during positive acceleration, closing cam during negative). Keep lash visible but tiny. Camshaft turns at half crank speed in a 4-stroke engine.

name: Geneva drive
summary: A pin on a constantly turning crank enters a slot and steps a slotted wheel a quarter turn, then a locking disc holds it still.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 90° of crank, dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, crank (arm with pin and locking disc), slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking arc contact alternate

explain.motion: The crank turns continuously; its pin enters a slot tangentially, drives the wheel through a quarter turn and leaves tangentially. While the pin is out, a raised locking disc on the crank sits in a concave arc on the wheel and holds it still. With 4 slots the wheel moves during 90° of crank rotation and rests for 270°.
explain.forces: The pin pushes on the slot wall; torque on the wheel is highest mid-index when the pin is closest to the wheel centre. Acceleration jumps at entry and exit, so impact and wear grow quickly with speed.
explain.benefits: Positive indexing and locking with very few parts, and the entry and exit have zero wheel velocity.
explain.limits: Infinite jerk at entry and exit limits speed, and the index angle is fixed by the slot count. The ratio of motion to dwell cannot be chosen freely.

build.ground: plate with crank axis O at (0,0) and wheel axis W at (110,0)
build.input: crank (disc plus arm), continuous rotation about O, belt-driven from a pulley

members.def: arm O to pin R, length a = c sin(pi/4) = 77.8 mm; pin radius 5.5 mm
locking disc on crank, radius 0.65 a = 50.6 mm, with relief cut-out facing the pin
4 radial slots, slot half-width 7 mm; slot mouth radius R = c cos(pi/4) = 77.8 mm; concave locking arcs between slots

params.name: R
params.note: wheel radius at slot mouth = c cos(pi/n)

build.notes: Wheel turns opposite to crank. Locking disc relief must clear the wheel tips during engagement; site computes it from the intersection of radius rhoD = Rw + 3 around W. Show dwell with a tag.

name: Internal Geneva drive
summary: A crank pin works inside a cup-shaped slotted wheel, stepping it the same way as the crank with a longer, gentler move and shorter dwell.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 270° of crank, dwell 90°

topology.notes: ground, crank with pin and locking cam, internal slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking contact alternate

explain.motion: The slotted wheel is a cup with slots pointing inward from its rim; the crank sits inside the cup with its axis offset from the wheel axis. The pin enters a slot tangentially and drives the wheel the same way as the crank for 270° of crank rotation, then a locking cam on the crank holds the wheel for the remaining 90°.
explain.forces: Since the move is spread over a longer crank angle, peak angular acceleration is much lower than in an external Geneva of the same slot count. The crank must be overhung (supported on one side only) because the wheel surrounds it.
explain.benefits: Smoother motion with lower peak acceleration, same-direction rotation and a compact package.
explain.limits: Dwell is short (less than half the cycle), and the overhung crank limits load. Hard to make with few slots because the pin path must fit inside the cup.

build.ground: plate with wheel axis W at (0,0) and crank axis O at (40,0) inside the wheel
build.output: internal slotted wheel angle about W

members.def: O to pin P, length a = c sin(pi/4) = 28.3 mm; pin dia 8 mm
convex locking sector on crank, radius 16 mm, opposite the pin
cup ring, rim inner radius 76, outer 88; 4 slots pointing inward from rim, inner slot end at radius c cos(pi/4) = 28.3 mm; concave locking arcs between slot roots

build.defining_relations: Tangential entry: a = c sin(pi/n). Crank angle in motion = 180° + 360°/n = 270°; dwell = 180° - 360°/n = 90°. Pin distance from W reaches c + a = 68.3 mm, so slots run from about 28 mm to beyond 72 mm radius. Wheel angle while engaged: tan(beta) = a sin(alpha)/(c + a cos(alpha)) measured from the line of centres.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; wheel steps 90° per crank turn, moving 270° and dwelling 90°
build.plot: wheel angle vs crank angle (staircase with long gentle risers), compare with external Geneva
build.notes: Wheel and crank rotate the same direction. Draw the crank overhung in front of the wheel web. Locking sector must swing clear of the slot roots while the pin is engaged.

name: Intermittent gear
summary: A gear with only a few teeth drives a full gear part of each turn; between bursts a locking rim holds the driven gear still.

ratio.typical: 90° per driver turn (5 of 20 teeth), dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, mutilated driver with locking disc, driven gear with locking arcs; gear mesh and locking contact alternate

explain.motion: The driver has teeth on only part of its rim. While those teeth are in mesh, the driven gear turns at the normal gear ratio; when they pass, a plain locking disc on the driver rides in a concave arc on the driven gear and holds it still. Here 5 of 20 teeth advance the driven gear a quarter turn per driver turn.
explain.forces: During mesh it acts like an ordinary spur pair at a 20° pressure angle. The first tooth hits the driven gear at full pitch-line speed, so there is a shock at engagement that grows with speed.
explain.benefits: Any step size and dwell split can be set by tooth count, and the driven gear is positively located throughout.
explain.limits: Sudden start and stop cause impact, so it suits slow or light duty. Geneva or cam indexers are preferred at high speed or load.

build.ground: plate with driver axis O1 at (0,0) and driven axis O2 at (80,0)
build.input: driver gear, continuous rotation about O1

members.def: module 4, z = 20 pitch spacing, only 5 consecutive teeth cut; pitch radius 40; locking disc radius 36 on the rest
module 4, z = 20 full teeth, pitch radius 40; locking plate with 4 concave arcs radius 36.5 between tooth groups

build.defining_relations: Index angle per driver turn = 360° x nT/z2 = 90°. Driver moves the output for 360° x nT/z1 = 90°, dwell 270°. Number of stops per driven turn = z2/nT = 4 (must be an integer). Centre distance cd = m(z1+z2)/2.
build.range: driver 360° continuous; driven steps 90° per driver turn
build.plot: driven angle vs driver angle (staircase with straight risers)
build.notes: Driven turns opposite to driver. Site's kinematic model lets the first and last teeth overlap slightly in plan; real designs thin or shorten the end teeth. Effective mesh angle uses eff(u) clamp to nT pitches.

name: Roller gear cam indexer
summary: A tapered rib cam on a constantly turning shaft steps a turret of rollers by one station, then locks it between the ribs.

ratio.typical: 45° per index (8 stops), index in 120° of camshaft, dwell 240°

topology.notes: ground, globoidal cam shaft, turret with radial rollers; two rollers in contact with the rib at all times (preloaded)

explain.motion: The input camshaft turns at constant speed. A raised rib wraps part way round a waisted (globoidal) cam; in its straight section it holds two turret rollers and the turret dwells, and in its twisted section it pushes the rollers along, rotating the turret one station. One cam turn gives one index.
explain.forces: Rollers are preloaded against both rib flanks, so there is no backlash and the turret is locked during dwell. Torque passes through rolling contact, and the cam law (modified sine) keeps peak acceleration and jerk low.
explain.benefits: High precision, high speed and no backlash, with smooth motion set by the cam law. Very rigid locking in dwell.
explain.limits: Expensive to make, fixed stop count and index time once cut, and needs a clutch or brake for overload. Bulky compared with a Geneva for light loads.

build.ground: housing with camshaft axis horizontal and turret axis vertical, offset by centre distance C

members.def: globoidal rib cam, throat radius about 40 mm, rib dwell segment over 240°, twisted index segment over 120°
disc with 8 radial rollers at pitch radius 60 mm, 45° apart
dia 20 mm cam followers on radial studs

params.name: C
params.note: centre distance between camshaft and turret axes

build.defining_relations: Turret angle phi = (360°/n) x s(theta/beta_index) during index, constant during dwell. Modified sine law: velocity coefficient Cv = 1.76, acceleration Ca = 5.53. Rib geometry is the envelope of roller cylinders swept by the turret motion about the turret axis, at centre distance C.
build.range: camshaft 360° continuous; turret 45° per cam turn, moving 120° and dwelling 240°
build.plot: turret angle vs camshaft angle, with velocity and acceleration curves
build.notes: Pseudo-3D: show the cam side-on with rib and the turret plan view. Two adjacent rollers straddle the rib in dwell; during index one roller leaves while the next enters. Axes are perpendicular and non-intersecting.

name: Ratchet and pawl
summary: A rocking lever's pawl pushes a toothed wheel forward one tooth per stroke while a second pawl stops it slipping back.

ratio.typical: one tooth (30°, 12 teeth) per lever stroke of 36°

topology.notes: ground, lever, ratchet wheel, driving pawl, holding pawl; pawl tips contact wheel teeth; springs keep pawls engaged (pawl angles follow the wheel)

explain.motion: The lever swings back and forth about the wheel axis. On the forward stroke its driving pawl catches the steep face of a tooth and pushes the wheel one tooth; on the return stroke it rides up over the sloped backs of the teeth. A holding pawl on the frame drops into each tooth to stop the wheel running back.
explain.forces: Load passes through the pawl tip on the steep tooth face; the face is undercut slightly so the pawl is pulled into engagement under load. The small backward movement before the holding pawl catches is the backlash, at most one tooth pitch.
explain.benefits: Simple, robust one-way drive and lock that can hold heavy loads.
explain.limits: Noisy, motion is in discrete steps, and backlash up to one pitch. Shock loads at engagement wear tooth faces and pawl tips.

build.ground: frame with wheel axis O at (0,0) and holding pawl pivot H at radius 75.1 mm, angle about -32°
build.input: lever, oscillating about O from 62° to 98° (36° stroke)

members.def: 12 sawtooth teeth, root radius 50, tip radius 62; steep face spans 3°, back slope 27°
arm length 128 mm about O; pawl pivot D at radius Rp = hypot(50, 56) = 75.1 mm
beak length 56 mm from pivot D to tip, tip face 32° bevel, spring-loaded toward wheel
same beak, pivot H fixed on frame, spring-loaded

params.name: Rp
params.note: pawl pivot radius from wheel centre

build.defining_relations: Wheel advance per stroke = 360°/N = 30° when lever stroke >= pitch + overtravel. Pawl pivot placed so the tip contact is tangent-ish: Rp = sqrt(r_root^2 + L^2), so the pawl line is tangent to the root circle at engagement. Pawl self-engages under load when the line from pivot to tip lies inside the tooth face normal (friction angle condition).
build.range: lever oscillates 36°; wheel advances 30° per cycle, one-way, dwelling on the return stroke
build.notes: Pawl angle solved each frame by bisection so its tip rests on the tooth profile. Show the pawl clicking over tips on the return stroke. Lever moves forward during first half of the cycle (osc from lo to hi).

examples.detail: A pawl and fine-toothed gear let the handle swing back without turning the bolt.

name: Sprag clutch
summary: Tilted figure-eight sprags between two races slip one way and wedge the other, so torque passes in one direction only.

ratio.typical: 1:1 when locked; free when the outer race overruns

topology.notes: ground, inner race, outer race, one sprag (in practice 12 to 30 sprags in a cage with a garter spring); two friction contacts per sprag

explain.motion: Each sprag is a short strut slightly longer than the gap between the races, tilted by a light spring. When the inner race tries to turn faster than the outer in the driving direction, friction tips the sprags upright so they wedge and lock the races together. In the other direction the sprags lean over and slide, letting the outer race overrun freely.
explain.forces: Torque goes through many sprags in compression across the gap, so capacity is high for the size. Locking depends on the gripping angle staying below the friction angle (typically 3° to 5° against a friction coefficient around 0.1).
explain.benefits: Engages almost instantly with very little backlash and runs silently when overrunning, unlike a pawl ratchet.
explain.limits: Relies on friction and race hardness; wrong lubricant or worn races can let it slip or roll over. Drag and wear when overrunning at high speed.

build.ground: housing supporting inner and outer races on a common axis O
build.input: inner race, rotation about O (driving direction counterclockwise)
build.output: outer race rotation about O; locked or overrunning state

members.def: inner race radius 20 mm
outer race bore radius 28 mm (gap 8 mm)
16 figure-eight sprags, diagonal length 8.4 mm, contact surfaces as arcs of radius about 4.5 mm
garter spring tilting all sprags toward engagement

params.name: L_sprag
params.note: sprag diagonal, slightly longer than the gap

params.name: grip_angle
params.note: strut angle at lock, must be < atan(mu)

build.defining_relations: Lock condition: tan(grip_angle) < mu (about 5.7° for mu = 0.1). Gap g = ro - ri; sprag tilt from radial theta satisfies L cos(theta) = g at contact. Driving: w_outer = w_inner when inner leads in the driving sense; otherwise w_outer free (w_outer >= w_inner).
build.range: inner race continuous; outer race follows 1:1 in drive, free to overrun the other way
build.plot: outer race speed vs inner race speed over a cycle with overrun (shows lock and freewheel regions)
build.notes: Animate a few sprags enlarged. Show tilt changing a few degrees between lock and overrun. Two-DOF when freewheeling: drive the inner race and let the outer race either follow or coast with decay.

name: Star wheel and pin
summary: A finger on a turning shaft knocks a star wheel on by one tooth per turn, and a sprung jumper snaps it into place and holds it.

ratio.typical: 36° per driver turn (10 teeth); 31 teeth for a date wheel

topology.notes: ground, driver with finger pin, star wheel, jumper lever with roller; finger-star and jumper-star contacts; jumper spring

explain.motion: A driver turns continuously and once per turn its finger enters a gap of the star wheel and pushes one tooth. A spring-loaded jumper rides up the tooth flank and, once the tooth passes its peak, snaps the star forward into the next gap. Between pushes the jumper holds the star still.
explain.forces: The finger works against the jumper spring until the tooth tip passes, then the spring does the last part of the step. The finger load is light but the snap gives a small impact and holding force depends entirely on the spring.
explain.benefits: Very simple, cheap and compact, with a crisp, well-defined rest position. The output can step through any number of positions per revolution.
explain.limits: Holding is only spring force, so it suits light loads and slow rates. Backdriving with enough force can jump the jumper.

build.ground: plate with driver axis O1 at (0,0), star axis O2 at (28,0) and jumper pivot J at (40,22)

members.def: disc with finger pin dia 3 mm at radius 12 mm
10 pointed teeth, tip radius 20 mm, root radius 14 mm, 60° tooth angle
lever from J, length 22 mm, roller or V-nose dia 4 mm seated in star gap
leaf spring pressing jumper toward star, preload about 1 N

build.defining_relations: Index per driver turn = 360°/N. Finger path circle (radius rf about O1) must reach inside the star tip circle: c - rf < r_tip, overlap 4 mm here. The finger must push the star at least half a pitch (180°/N) past the jumper peak so the spring completes the step. Jumper rest position at a gap bisector.
build.range: driver 360° continuous; star steps 36° once per driver turn, finger engagement about 60° of driver angle including the jumper snap
build.plot: star angle vs driver angle (staircase; finger push then a fast snap)
build.notes: Model in two phases: finger-driven (star follows finger contact) up to the tooth tip passing the jumper, then snap (animate quickly to the next detent). Star turns opposite to driver.

examples.detail: A 31-tooth date star is advanced once a day by a finger on the 24-hour wheel and held by a jumper.
